The Council will now consider draft proposal L.26, entitled Responding to the Human Rights and Humanitarian Crisis Caused by the Ongoing Armed Conflict in the Sudan. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom to introduce the draft text.

Thank you, Mr. President. On behalf of a core group of Germany, Ireland, the Netherlands, Norway and the United Kingdom, I present draft resolution L26, which responds to the human rights and humanitarian crisis in Sudan. Mr. President, the fact-finding mission's report paints a devastating picture. Communities shattered, millions displaced, and civilians trapped in a cycle of violence. Drone warfare conducted by both the Rapid Support Forces and the Sudanese Armed Forces has extended the geographical reach of hostilities. Attacks on hospitals, markets, even a kindergarten, have left civilians with nowhere safe to go. Illegal flows of weapons and external support are enabling these atrocities, wreaking havoc across the region and undermining prospects for peace. It is imperative that states and other external actors cease arming, financing, and otherwise sustaining this devastating conflict. The Core Group calls for accountability across the full chain of responsibility and via every avenue available. In this context, we commend the critical work of the International Criminal Court to ensure accountability and justice for victims of atrocities in Sudan, and call for full Sudanese cooperation with the Court. Faced with unconscionable horrors across Sudan, this Council cannot look away. We must stand united. The UN Fact-Finding Mission is the only independent investigative body documenting and reporting on these violations and abuses across Sudan. We welcome its commitment to work in step with other independent accountability efforts, in particular the joint fact-finding mission of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights. The Banjul Joint Declaration in May of this year is testimony to the collaboration and complementarity between the UN mechanism and the African Union, whose leadership remains crucial to ending the conflict. Renewing the fact-finding mission's mandate is essential to enable justice in Sudan and lay the groundwork for future accountability. Throughout the session, we have held consultations and discussed this draft extensively with all delegations, starting with Sudan. We took on board many of the proposals made, including a number from Sudan itself. Yet, despite our best efforts, it is regretful that these changes were not enough for the Sudanese authorities, as this is a resolution very much for the people of Sudan. We reiterate the Banjul joint declaration's recognition of the courage and resilience of victims, survivors and human rights defenders across Sudan who remain committed to peace and documentation efforts, often at great personal risk. These brave actors deserve more than this Council's attention. They deserve our solidarity. We urge all members to stand with the people of Sudan and vote in favour of this resolution. Thank you.

Thank you. I've been informed by the Secretariat that there are six additional co-sponsors. I now give the floor to members of the Council who wish to make general comments. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of North Macedonia.

Thank you, Mr. President. We thank the Core Group for presenting draft resolution L.26 in response to the human rights and humanitarian crisis caused by the ongoing armed conflict in Sudan. More than three years since the start of the armed conflict, the situation in Sudan remains deeply alarming. Over 33 million people need humanitarian assistance. Tens of millions have been displaced. Approximately 20 million people are experiencing severe levels of food insecurity. The Council has repeatedly raised its concern about the serious human rights violations in Sudan. We have an important preventive role to play in addressing the emerging risks, preventing further deterioration, and contributing to the environment conducive to the protection of civilians in respect for human rights in the country. First and foremost, an immediate ceasefire is needed towards a lasting solution to the conflict, followed by inclusive, transparent, and credible political process. Accountability for human rights violation, in particular sexual and gender-based violence, must be at the core of any sustainable peace process. Mr. President, the resolution before us reflects the devastating humanitarian situation and the grave human rights violations and abuses committed by all parties to the conflict. The fact-finding mission has documented cases of killings, enforced disappearances, sexual and gender-based violence, violence against children, arbitrary arrest and detention, and the mass displacement of civilians. Its findings also raise serious concerns about the use of drones, causing devastating and disproportionate harm to civilian population, including women and children. We support the extension of the mandate of the fact-finding mission for a period of one year. Its work is indispensable to support further national accountability efforts and investigations. Its mandate should continue with the full cooperation with all parties to the conflict. We also welcome all efforts aimed in this escalating facilities protecting civilians and ensuring humanitarian access. Civilians must be able to move freely and have safe and unhindered access to the basic services and humanitarian assistance they need. Thank you.

Mr. President,

Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Japan, followed by Kenya.

Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Kenya, followed by the Netherlands.

Thank you, Mr. President. Kenya remains concerned by the continuing suffering of the Sudanese people and reiterate our call on all parties to agree to an immediate ceasefire without preconditions. All parties must fully respect their obligation under international humanitarian law and international human rights law. The protection of civilians, including women, children, humanitarian personnel, and other vulnerable groups must remain paramount, and attacks against civilian objects and critical infrastructure must cease. We further underscore the urgent need for a full, safe, rapid, and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout the Sudan. Humanitarian actors must be able to reach civilians in need without obstruction, and essential assistance must be allowed to reach all affected populations. Kenya reiterates that there can be no military solution to the conflict. A durable political resolution remains urgent and must be anchored on a Sudanese-led and Sudanese-owned process. that is inclusive, credible, and responsive to the aspiration of the Sudanese people. Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Netherlands, followed by South Africa.

Thank you, Mr. President. South Africa takes the floor to deliver general comments on resolution L/26. President, independent investigation and documentation of violations, including the preservation of evidence, are essential to combat impunity. Urgent protection and accountability is vital. In addition to Sudan's cooperation with three UN mechanisms, L26 itself has acknowledged the establishment of National Investigative Commission. Thank you, Mr. President. The Gambia's vote on draft resolution L26 today is guided by our overriding consideration for the millions of victims of the war in Sudan, who continue to bear the devastating consequences of this conflict, and the need for complementary pathways for justice and accountability. Behind the reports of killings, displacement, sexual violence, attacks on civilian infrastructure, lie real people, women and men, girls and boys, older persons, persons with disabilities, and entire communities whose rights and freedoms have been profoundly violated with impunity. These victims and survivors have a right to truth and justice. They have a right to know what happened, to have serious violations properly documented and investigated, and ultimately to hold all perpetrators to account. Our own national experience of confronting the painful legacy of authoritarianism through truth-seeking, accountability, and reparations has reinforced our conviction that sustainable peace cannot be built in Sudan if any of the serious violations and abuses of human rights go unaddressed. In our view, truth, justice, and accountability are the foundation on which sustainable peace and reconciliation must be constructed. Different areas of Sudan remain in the hands of either the government of Sudan or the RSF. External forces continue to fuel the war with supply of arms, ammunition, and drones, with little regard for international law. Therefore, there is a need for complementary and independent documentation of the crimes being committed in Sudan, the preservation of evidence, and the establishment of facts for future accountability. This work is important to ensure that victims of the conflict are not denied justice and accountability. The Gambia continues to attach great importance to national and African-led accountability processes. We have previously abstained from the vote on this resolution. However, the Banjul Joint Declaration signed between the African Commission and the fact-finding mission adds an important layer of complementarity of international and regional efforts to address the human rights situation in Sudan in a balanced manner. Our support for the renewal of the mandate should neither be interpreted as diminishing Sudan's sovereignty or territorial integrity, nor a slight on its National Investigation Commission. Rather, it reflects our conviction that circumstances on the ground require a combination of national, regional, and international efforts to create credible pathways towards justice and sustainable peace. The protection of civilians and the establishment of the truth and meaningful accountability must remain an integral part of that path. On this basis, the President that the Gambia will vote in favor of draft resolution L26 for the renewal of the mandate of the fact-finding mission. Thank you.

Thank you. I see no further request for explanation of vote before the vote. At the request of the delegation of China and Egypt, the Council will now proceed to a recorded vote on draft resolution L26. I now ask the Secretariat to open the voting machine. And I request all delegations to register their vote. Please check that your vote is correctly reflected. All right. The voting is now closed. The result of the recorded vote are as follow. In favour 28, against 10, and 9 abstention. Draft proposal L26 is therefore adopted. A copy of the results of the vote will shortly be uploaded to the HRC portal. We will now move on to explanations of vote and general comments after the vote on all resolutions adopted under agenda item 2. Any delegation wishing to take the floor? Any request? UK? UK, you have the floor, please.

Thank you, Mr. President. We would like to make a statement after the vote on adopted resolution L8. Since the Taliban's return to power, women and girls have faced systematic restrictions on their rights in Afghanistan, denying them agency over almost every aspect of their lives. For decades, Afghan women have played a central role in Afghanistan's public life. They have been members of parliament and served in the cabinet. After 2001, Afghan women served across society as judges, teachers, journalists, civil servants, health workers, and community leaders. These gains were built by Afghan women. They represented years of courage, determination, and public service, yet they have been dismantled by force. The Afghan woman who once sat in a parliament, stood in a courtroom, taught in a classroom, healed the sick in a hospital or served her community is now being told to disappear from the society she sustained. For Afghan girls, the denial of their rights today, including the barring of their education, is the theft of opportunity, independence and a future of their own. In the face of this deterioration, sustained international scrutiny is essential. So too is accountability. Impunity for violations and abuses of human rights and for violations of international humanitarian law cannot continue. We welcome the resolution's strong focus on the rights of women and girls and its renewal of the special rapporteur's mandate. We thank the EU for their leadership on this critical initiative. The UK did not co-sponsor last year's resolution due to reservations with certain modalities of the new mechanism established. Those reservations remain, but our co-sponsorship this year reflects the profoundly disturbing and deteriorating human rights situation in Afghanistan. We stand with the women and girls of Afghanistan until they can again exercise their rights and participate fully in society. We will continue to work with partners to defend the human rights of all Afghans, including LGBT+ persons and members of ethnic and religious minorities. and hold those responsible for violations and abuses to account. Thank you.

Thank you. I don't see any further requests for explanation of vote after the vote under agenda item 2. We now move to agenda item 3. The Council will now consider draft resolution L.1, entitled "The right to development". And I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Uganda, on behalf of the NAM, to introduce the draft resolution.

Thank you, Mr. President. Uganda has the honour to table resolution A/HRC/63/20. stroke L1 on behalf of the Nana Land Movement. We thank all states and civil society that constructively participated in the informal consultations to inform the outcome of the draft resolution tabled today. This draft resolution is largely composed of texts from the previously adopted resolution with some new language that is informed by the real-time development in the human rights field and the needs in the respective states. The new language was introduced in the resolution, amongst others, to acknowledge that States have the responsibility to protect and promote the enjoyment of the right to development. Additionally, the resolution emphasizes the importance of cooperation, especially amongst all States, while stressing that South-South cooperation should not affect the existing North-South cooperation to enable the continuation of the existing official development assistance commitments. Mr. President, this resolution also recognizes the biennial panel discussion that was held in commemoration of the 40th anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development last September. The discussion, chaired by yourself, Mr. President, afforded a significant opportunity for the international community to demonstrate and reiterate its unequivocal commitment to the right of development, including taking stock of the achievements, obstacles and challenges encountered over the past four decades in the implementation of the Declaration of the Right to Development at the national, regional and international levels. Finally, the resolution requests all public meetings of the Working Group on the Right to Development be webcast on the UN Web TV. This is in accordance with Council Decision 56/115 of 10 July 2024. The PBIs of webcasting the work of the working group is no different from the cost of all other working groups, and the minimal cost should not be reason to lose the enormous opportunity that it provides people around the world with direct, unfiltered access to global governance, human rights monitoring, and international policy making. We believe that human rights are universal, indivisible, interrelated, and mutually reinforcing, that under no circumstances should people be deprived of their basic means of survival or access to critical infrastructure, services, and goods that are enshrined in the right to development. We therefore invite all members of the Council to support and adopt the resolution by consensus, and if put to a vote, we implore all members to vote in favor of the resolution. I thank you, Mr. President.
Thank you. I now give the floor to members of the Council who wish to make general comments. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Egypt, followed by Cuba.

Mr. President, the delegation of Egypt supports draft resolution L.1, tabled by the NAM Group, regarding the right to development. The adoption of this draft resolution coincides with the 40th anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development, which requires us to renew our commitment to the principles embedded therein, foremost of which the entrenchment of the recognition of the right to development as an intrinsic and inalienable human right. The draft resolution acquires special importance in light of what development efforts are facing in terms of global and overlapping challenges that limit the ability of states to achieve development goals and invest in basic services that are tightly linked to the full enjoyment of human rights. We regret the persistent recourse to voting on a right that has been adopted and recognized by the international community for 40 years now. The failure to adopt this draft resolution by consensus begs a legitimate question about the message that the Human Rights Council is sending regarding the status of development within the human rights architecture. Can we even talk about the full enjoyment of human rights in the absence of development? Egypt affirms that development is an ongoing process that all peoples require, irrespective of the level of development, and promoting the right to development requires international cooperation that is based on partnership and the mutual respect for national priorities in such a way as to ensure that no one is left behind. In conclusion, we'd like to address the membership of this Council and say that adopting this draft resolution by consensus will send a unified message saying that we are fully committed to promoting the right to development and to translating that right into a lived reality that reflects positively on the livelihoods of peoples around the world. Thank you, President.
Thank you. I give the distinguished representative of Cuba, followed by Indonesia.

President, I would like to thank Uganda for presenting the draft resolution L.1 on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement. The Council of the General Assembly acknowledged the right to development 40 years ago as an inalienable and universal human right. Nevertheless, for the vast majority of countries of the Global South, this right continues to be aspirational a chimera. This is very worrying because the right to development is an umbrella right. That means to say that achieving this right is absolutely vital for enjoying other human rights. Cuba supports the swift adoption by the General Assembly of an International Covenant on the Right to Development based on the text recommended by the Council in 2023. The Covenant would place that right on the same level as other human rights as tangible and enforceable obligations at international level. Unilateral coercive measures, such as the criminal blockade that the United States is imposing on Cuba, are incompatible with human rights, and such measures must be halted, as is the case of draft resolution L.1, The Council must integrate the right to development in its work transparently and systematically. Special procedures, mandate holders and all other Council mechanisms must integrate the perspective of the right to development in their discharge of their mandates. Cuba calls upon other Member States to support this draft resolution L1 and vote in favour of it. Thank you very much, President.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Indonesia, followed by Ethiopia.

Thank you, Mr. President. We thank Uganda for its continued leadership in presenting this important draft resolution on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement. This regular initiative reaffirms the importance of the right to development as an integrating framework for the comprehensive realization and indivisibility of all human rights, including civil, political, economic, social, and cultural rights. Today, countries in both the global South and the global North confront developmental and human rights challenges of their own. Even in advanced economies, millions of people remain at risk of poverty and social exclusion. The right to development is therefore universally relevant, and its realization is a shared responsibility of all States without exception. Mr. President, Indonesia reiterates a strong commitment to the operationalization of the right to development at the international level, including through an early adoption of the draft International Covenant on the Right to Development now before the General Assembly. To support the ongoing process in New York, we stand ready to work more closely with other delegations to bridge divergent views and enhance coordination between Geneva and New York. This deliberation requires openness, flexibility, and constructive engagement from all sides. Divergence of views must not prevent us from moving this process forward aimed at strengthening the realization of the right to development. Having said that, the adoption of the text before us is one concrete way to sustain the momentum and advance us towards that objective. For these reasons, Indonesia urges all members of the Council to support draft resolution L.1 And should a vote be called, to vote in favor. I thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ethiopia, followed by Pakistan.

Thank you, Mr. President. Ethiopia commends Uganda for its leadership and constructive efforts in advancing this important resolution. The realization of the right to development is central to advancing the full enjoyment of human rights and fundamental freedoms. It calls for an enabling environment in which all individuals and peoples can participate meaningfully in, continue to, and benefit from development with equality, dignity, and justice. We therefore welcome the resolution's emphasis on international cooperation on the full enjoyment and effective implementation of the SDGs. We believe that advancing the right to development and achieving the Sustainable Development Goals are mutually reinforcing objectives, particularly in addressing poverty, inequality, and the persistent structural barriers that continue to constrain the development prospects of many developing countries. Ethiopia also welcomes the continued engagement of the Working Group and the Expert Mechanism and the Special Rapporteur on the Right to Development. Their respective contributions are important in strengthening dialogue, sharing expertise and translating the principles of the right to development into meaningful and tangible outcomes for people and communities. We also attach particular importance to the ongoing process towards a legally binding instrument on the right to development. Ethiopia remains fully committed to the realization of the right to development for all. We believe that development, peace, human rights, and international cooperation are mutually reinforcing the pillars of a more just, equitable, and inclusive international order. In this spirit, Ethiopia calls upon all esteemed members of this Council to support the adoption of this resolution by consensus. Should the resolution be put to a vote, Ethiopia urges all esteemed members of the Human Rights Council to vote in favour of the resolution. Thank you, Mr. President.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Pakistan.

Thank you, Mr. President. Pakistan welcomes the draft resolution contained in document L.1, titled "The Right to Development," and thanks the delegation of Uganda in its capacity as the chair of the Non-Aligned Movement for introducing it for this Council's consideration. Mr. President, 40 years ago, the Declaration on the Right to Development placed human beings at the center of development, affirming that the right to development was an inalienable human right of individuals and peoples. Its message was profound. Progress must not merely create wealth, it must advance social development and uphold human dignity. Regrettably, that promise confronts a stark reality across much of the developing world. Debt servicing consumes scarce resources that should be directed towards development. Natural disasters are erasing hard-won gains. Technological inequalities threaten to carry old divides into a new digital age. Accelerating reform of the international financial architecture, meeting the pledges made towards official development assistance, Operationalizing the climate loss and damage fund and bridging digital divides therefore remain key. A right cannot be realized where the means to realize it are denied. We therefore appreciate the work of this Council's mechanisms on the right to development in fostering greater appreciation and understanding. In that same spirit, my delegation supports the early adoption of the International Covenant on the Right to Development. Mr. President, the measure of development is not only how far one individual or group advances, but whether humanity advances together. We extend our support to draft resolution L.1 and join other delegations in calling on the Council to adopt it by consensus. If it were put to a vote, Pakistan would vote in favor and urges all others to do the same. I thank you.

Thank you. I've been informed by the Secretariat that there are PBIs for this draft resolution. The corresponding PBI oral statement has been made available on the HRC portal. I now give the floor to members of the Council who wish to make explanations or vote before the vote on draft resolution L.1. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of the UK.

Mr. President, The United Kingdom thanks the delegation of Uganda on behalf of the NAM for their engagement on this resolution. The UK remains firmly committed to sustainable development, poverty reduction and the promotion and protection of all human rights. We recognize that sustainable development plays an important role in enabling individuals to enjoy their human rights and fulfill their potential. It is the UK's long-standing position that the right to development is best realized through the implementation of existing international human rights obligations. We are therefore concerned that this resolution seeks to advance the development of a new legally binding instrument on the right to development. We do not consider such an instrument necessary given the extensive existing international human rights framework. Further, we are clear that it is individuals who are rights holders and states who are duty bearers. We are concerned that this resolution places increasing emphasis on obligations and processes between States, rather than on the individual as the holder of the right to development. While we appreciate the engagement of the NAM throughout informals, these concerns unfortunately remain unresolved. For these reasons, the United Kingdom will call a vote on this resolution and will vote against. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Estonia, followed by Japan.

Thank you, Mr. President. I have the honor to speak again on behalf of the European Union member states that are members of the Human Rights Council. This explanation of vote has been agreed by the EU as a whole. For the European Union, development is an inalienable universal right, indivisible from human dignity. The Declaration on the Right to Development puts individuals as the central actors, drivers and beneficiaries of development. States, as duty bearers, carry the primary responsibility for realising all human rights, including the right to development. The EU promotes a human rights-based approach to inclusive and sustainable development. We work towards achieving sustainable development the non-discriminatory realization of all human rights, eradicating poverty in all its dimensions, tackling discrimination and inequalities, and leaving no one behind. We also act on our commitment. The European Union and its Member States remain the world's largest official development assistance donors. Mr. President, the EU therefore thanks Uganda for leading on behalf of NAM open and inclusive informal consultations on resolution L.1. We participated constructively to ensure that the text aligns with the principle of universality of human rights, with individuals as rights holders and states as duty bearers. Despite diverging views on the right to development, particularly on a draft legally binding instrument, The European Union has and will continue to engage constructively. We appreciate the efforts made to address some of our concerns and are encouraged by the constructive developments. We are still concerned by the approach that ignores the international human rights law that defines human rights as rights of individuals, including with regard to the right to development. Although the EU cannot support resolution L1, it thanks the pen holder for constructive dialogue during negotiations and remains ready to be actively engaged in a meaningful discussion with the NAM and the wider UN membership on this important issue. I thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Japan, followed by Iceland.

Thank you, Mr. President. At the outset, we thank the NAM for presenting this resolution. Japan has been providing official development assistance, ODA, for more than 70 years. Over the decades, we have supported 190 countries and regions, contributing to healthcare, high-quality infrastructure development, education, and capacity building. We firmly recognize the importance of development as one of the three pillars of the United Nations. However, while states have the primary responsibility for the full realization of all human rights, every individual person must always be recognized as a rights holder, regardless of where they live. Unfortunately, this draft resolution appears to place greater emphasis on the interests of states rather than individuals in the context of the right to development. We cannot support an approach that prioritizes the development processes over the protection and promotion of human rights. We recognize that there are differing views regarding the right to development. In particular, with respect to the legally binding instrument referenced in this draft resolution, further substantive discussions are necessary, and their conclusions should not be prejudged. For these reasons, we call for a vote and will vote against draft resolution L1. We encourage other members to do the same. I thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Iceland, followed by Spain.

Mr. President, Iceland reaffirms its support for development as an integral part of the human rights framework. and its commitment to the full implementation of the 2030 Agenda. In addition to the important premise of the 2030 Agenda to leave no one behind, the Vienna Declaration affirms that democracy, development, and respect for human rights are interdependent and mutually reinforcing, and it remains the foundation of our approach. It is on the same basis that we continue to seek a common understanding among states on development. Our concerns regarding specific references, including references to a legally binding instrument, have not yet been addressed in the text. We raise them now, not to detract from the purpose of the resolution, but to clarify the basis for our abstention. Iceland's abstention is an expression of continued engagement, not of disengagement. We are grateful for the openness with which the Core Group and Uganda, on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement, received our views. We hope that in future iterations of the draft resolution, the text may develop in a way that allows a broader group of delegations to join in. For these reasons, Iceland will abstain on the vote on the draft resolution L.1. I thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Spain, followed by China.

Thank you very much, President. Spain subscribes to the EU statement and would like to add a certain number of comments in our national capacity to explain our vote on draft resolution L1. Spain would like to thank the work of the Non-Aligned Movement and Uganda in particular for promoting this initiative. The right to development is an integral part of the universal framework of human rights and must be achieved in full consistency with the universality, indivisibility and interdependence of all human rights. Now, our position is based on a premise which I've also heard echoed by other speakers. Unless you have appropriate funding, human rights, particularly economic, social and cultural rights, including the right to development, will not be fully achieved. The Seville Commitment set that out quite clearly and put development at the heart of its aims and provided a solid framework for the policies to achieve the right to development. International law, individuals as right holders and recognition of existing frameworks such as the Seville Commitment must be put at the heart of the text of the resolution before us. So Spain is unable to support the resolution in its current form, but we will continue to work constructively in order to support the right to development, the work of the Council on the subject, including in future negotiations, and also to support the approach of the human rights economy, which is endorsed by the Office of the High Commissioner. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of China.

Mr. President, I would like to commend Uganda for once again tabling L1 on behalf of NAM. Forty years ago, the Declaration on the Right to Development clearly stated that the right to development is an inalienable human right. Regrettably, however, mounting challenges such as geopolitical conflicts, North-South divide, and governance deficit are adding hurdles to its realization. All countries should seize the occasion of this 40th anniversary to take effective measures to create an environment for equitable development and jointly meet development challenges. The right to development is reflected in all other human rights. It is both an individual right and a collective right for all countries and peoples. We must abide by a correct human rights approach, give full recognition and equal weight to the right to development, and eliminate poverty and inequality so as to enhance the basis for human rights governance. The Chinese people have undertaken tremendous efforts and achieved huge success in pursuit of development and the right to development. will be guided by the Global Development Initiative and work steadily to make this right enjoyable and accessible to all. Mr. President, on the occasion of the 40th anniversary of the adoption of the Declaration on the Right to Development, the Human Rights Council is now deciding to put a vote to this resolution on the right to development. We are deeply saddened by this. This also shows the double standards and hypocrisy of some countries on the issues with human rights. We will vote in favor and would like to call on other members to do likewise. I thank you, Mr. President.

Thank you. I see no further request for explanation of vote before the vote. At the request of the delegations of UK and Japan, the Council will now proceed to a recorded vote on draft resolution L.1. I now ask the Secretariat to open the voting machine. And I request all delegations to register their votes. Please ensure that your votes are correctly reflected. And I now ask the Secretariat to close the voting machine and the voting is now closed. The results of the recorded votes are as follows. 28 in favour, 14 against and 5 abstention. Draft proposal L1 is therefore adopted. A copy of the results of the vote will shortly be uploaded to the portal. The Council will now consider draft resolution L.2, entitled "Mandate of Special Rapporteur on the negative impact of unilateral coercive measures on the enjoyment of human rights". I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Uganda, on behalf of the NAM, to introduce the draft text. You have the floor.

Uganda has the honor to table this resolution, A/HRC/63/L.2, on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement, NAM. We welcome the constructive engagement we had with all member states during the informal consultations. Despite the varying views on United Nations coercive measures, the NAM remains committed to dialogue with all partners towards possible consensus. This draft resolution is composed of streamlined text that requests the Council to extend the mandate of the Special Rapporteur on the negative impact of unilateral coercive measures on the enjoyment of human rights. Whereas there may be differing views regarding the thematic resolution on the negative impact of UCMs, we believe that the mandate holder will play an important role in enlightening us further on this important issue. We further believe that the Special Rapporteur will play an important role in examining the wide range of the impact of unilateral coercive measures on international humanitarian and human rights law, and on the economy, peace, security, and social fabric of States. Furthermore, the mandate holder will continue the work of developing a methodology to account for and continue to make visible the impact of unilateral coercive measures on the enjoyment of human rights. The resolution calls on governments to cooperate with and assist the Special Rapporteur in her tasks, to supply all necessary information requested by the mandate holder, and to respond favourably to requests for visits to enable her to fulfil her mandate effectively. Mr. President, UNATO coercive measures in the form of economic sanctions and the secondary sanctions have far-reaching implications on the enjoyment of human rights by the general population of targeted states. They disproportionately affect the poor and persons in the most vulnerable situations, and this only enhances the need for the extension of the mandate holder to continue shedding light and attention to this. It's against this background and our renewed commitment to champion the enjoyment of human rights by all that we invite all Council members to support and adopt this resolution. I thank you.

I've been informed by the Secretariat that there are no additional co-sponsors and I now give the floor to members of the council who wish to make general comments I give the floor to distinguished representative of Egypt followed by Cuba.

President first of all We'd like to thank the Ugandan delegation for having chaired the Non-Aligned Movement over the past three years, and we'd like to wish Uzbekistan every success as the incoming chair. We are the largest political grouping in the world with 120 member states. The Non-Aligned Movement continues to support a number of different international initiatives, notably the mandate of the special rapporteur on unilateral coercive measures. Our position is as follows. When sanctions or other unilateral measures are taken outside the framework of international law, they have long term impacts which are extremely serious. Unilateral coercive measures should not be used as mechanisms for exerting economic or political pressure on states. We oppose any unilateral coercive measures because they undermine the principles of the UN Charter and are in opposition to peaceful coexistence and non-interference. We applaud the efforts deployed to achieve a neutral text which would bring together different currents of opinion. This is the case of this text here. We appreciate the cooperative spirit of the negotiations on this draft resolution and we support Member States to support it. Egypt certainly will vote in favour if a vote is called. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Cuba, followed by Ethiopia.

President, we'd like to thank Uganda for introducing draft resolution L2 on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement. As the draft underscores, unilateral coercive measures are in opposition to the UN Charter, international law, international humanitarian law, and the rules and principles regulating peaceful coexistence among states. So this is why this mandate is more necessary than ever. This is because multilateralism and international law are under specific threat. The latest report from the Special Rapporteur, which is mentioned in the draft resolution, refers to her visit to Cuba. The visit report objectively documents the huge damage caused to the Cuban people by the criminal economic blockade and energy siege imposed by the United States. The report shows clear evidence as to how these measures violate Cubans human rights. Her report actually coincides with those of many other special procedures mandate holders. They've all called for this ineffective assault on Cuban rights. The United States must comply with the special rapporteur's recommendations, including the following: one, lift or suspend all unilateral coercive measures applied against Cuba; two, lift all restrictions on the supply of essential goods to Cuba, including food, medicines, and medical equipment, and restrictions on maintaining and developing critical infrastructure, such as electrical energy networks and water supply networks. Three, remove Cuba from the list of states allegedly supporting or sponsoring terrorism. and 4. Put an end to the national emergency which declares Cuba as a threat to the United States national security and 5. Choose the path of dialogue for resolving conflicts with Cuba. Cuba supports the request made in draft resolution L2 for providing the Special Rapporteur with all the necessary assistance, including sufficient human, technical and financial assistance necessary for the effective fulfilment of her mandate. Cuba calls on Member States to vote in favour of draft resolution L2. Thank you very much, President.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ethiopia.

Thank you, Mr. President. Ethiopia would like to express its appreciation to Uganda for its leadership and continued efforts on behalf of the non-aligned movement in advancing this important mandate, which remains highly relevant to strengthening the protection and promotion of human rights and addresses the adverse impact of unilateral coercive measures on their enjoyment. Ethiopia recognizes the importance of continued attention to the human rights implications of unilateral coercive measures, particularly where their effects may impair development and the full enjoyment of human rights. The protection and promotion of human rights must remain at the center of our collective efforts. At the same time, we must recognize that the realization of human rights, including the right to development, is closely connected to an enabling international environment based on cooperation, solidarity, sovereign equality, and respect for international law. Ethiopia is particularly concerned by the potential humanitarian and developmental consequences of measures that may adversely affect access to essential goods, services, finance, technology and international cooperation. Such impacts can place additional burdens on vulnerable populations and may constrain the ability of developing countries to advance their national development priorities. In this regard, Ethiopia welcomes the continued work of the Special Rapporteur in documenting and assessing the human rights implications of unilateral coercive measures and in promoting greater awareness, dialogue and accountability within the international human rights system. Mr. President, Ethiopia firmly believes that differences among states should be addressed through dialogue, negotiation, and peaceful means, consistent with the purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations. Multilateral cooperation remains essential to addressing global challenges and to ensuring that efforts to advance human rights and sustainable development are mutually reinforcing. In this spirit, Ethiopia calls upon all esteemed members of the Council to support the adoption of the draft resolution L2 by consensus. Should the draft resolution be put to a vote, Ethiopia urges all esteemed members of the Council to vote in favour. I thank you, Mr. President.

Thank you. I see no further requests for general comments. I have been informed by the Secretariat that there are PBIs for this draft resolution, and the required resources have already been included in the proposed programme budget. I now give the floor to members of the Council who wish to make explanations of vote before the vote on the draft resolution. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Estonia.

Mr. President, I have the honour to speak on behalf of the European Union member states that are members of the Human Rights Council. This explanation of vote has been agreed by the EU as a whole. The European Union thanks Uganda for leading the informal consultations on behalf of the NAM on this resolution. We especially appreciate the efforts by the Benelux to streamline and shorten the text, focusing on the mandate renewal itself and reflecting the focus already in the title of this resolution. Nevertheless, the European Union continues to oppose the fundamental premise of this resolution that all autonomous sanctions negatively impact the enjoyment of human rights. Mr. President, while we agree that states should refrain from illegal unilateral measures and their negative effects, we disagree with a narrative that treats temporary, targeted, and proportionate restrictive measures adopted in accordance with international law the same as illegal measures and arbitrary economic coercion. There is no general prohibition under international law of unilateral restrictive measures. Autonomous measures provide a peaceful and lawful tool to act, including when the UN's response to flagrant violations of international law is obstructed by the use of the veto. We remain ready to engage on this issue with the NAM, the wider UN membership, as well as the Special Rapporteur. Mr. President, European Union restrictive measures are designed to avoid as much as possible any unintended consequences. They can be challenged in court and have no extraterritorial application. The humanitarian carve-outs support the commitment to protecting people, including countries on the UN or autonomous sanctions. In this context, I would like to remind that the EU and its Member States remain the biggest donor of development and humanitarian assistance in the world. Taking this into account, the European Union cannot support the draft resolution L2 and calls for a vote on this resolution. The EU Member States that are members of the Human Rights Council will be voting against the resolution. I thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Japan.

Thank you, Mr. President. Japan thanks NAM for its efforts to prepare the draft resolution L2. Japan certainly shares the view that the theme of the draft resolution is important as a free and open international order based on the rule of law that we have fostered is facing profound challenges on multiple fronts. However, Japan cannot support assertions that all so-called UCMs are contrary to international law or constitute human rights violations in and of themselves. All sovereign nations have a legitimate right to take autonomous measures to address threats to international peace and security in full compliance with international law, including the UN Charter. Japan also reiterates that sanctions should not affect humanitarian activities. When applying sanctions, Japan and its partners include clear humanitarian exemptions to avoid negatively impacting humanitarian assistance. As the draft resolution does not differentiate between legitimate and illegitimate sanctions, Japan is unable to support the resolution. For these reasons, Japan will vote against draft resolution L2. Thank you, Mr. President.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Iceland, followed by the UK.

Mr. President, Iceland thanks the Core Group and you count on behalf of the non-aligned movement in particular for the openness and courtesy with which our views were received during the informal consultations on draft resolution L2. Iceland has engaged in good faith, and it is in that spirit that we explain our vote. Our position does not reflect indifference to the concerns that motivate this draft resolution. Iceland shares the concern over the negative impact that sanctions regimes can have on civilian populations, in particular through overcompliance and de-risking by financial and commercial actors. Security Council Resolution 2664 from 2022, as well as the humanitarian exemptions that have since been incorporated into many restrictive measures frameworks, including those that Iceland applies, demonstrate that this concern is shared across regions. In this regard, Iceland would welcome the opportunity to engage constructively on a text that reflects this. The term "unilateral coercive measures" has no agreed definition in international law, and that is primarily where our difficulty lies. Restrictive measures adopted in accordance with international law in response to serious violations are a legitimate instrument of foreign policy intended to respond to violations of international law and human rights, and demand that should not proceed from the presumption to the contrary. In this light, we note with interest the Special Rapporteur's acknowledgement in her latest report presented to this Council that a differentiated analysis of measures should underpin her work. We encourage the core group to consider how that approach might be reflected in future texts. For these reasons, Iceland will vote no on draft resolution L2. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative. of the UK, followed by Chile.

Mr. President, the United Kingdom thanks Uganda in their role as chair of the NAM for their engagement on this resolution. The UK cannot support the renewal of this mandate while it continues to rest on a misleading and inaccurate characterization of the UK's autonomous sanctions. The mandate has too often treated fundamentally different measures as though they were the same, and has failed to adequately distinguish between broad economic coercion and lawful, targeted sanctions with robust safeguards. UK sanctions are lawful, targeted, and transparent. They are used to deter and disrupt egregious conduct and to uphold international norms. They are transparent, include due process protections, the ability to seek review, humanitarian exemptions, and licensing provisions. They do not target essential food, medicines, or civilian populations. Sanctions can have unintended effects, and those effects should be examined carefully. Good afternoon, President. I'd like to begin by thanking all delegations that took part constructively in the consultations on this draft resolution. Well, we see that two major transformations are taking place at the same time. Our people are growing older and our lives are being placed online. Both processes provide new opportunities but also challenges for promoting and protecting human rights. The expansion of digital space have transformed the way in which we communicate, work, access services and take part in public life, but also they've created new forms of abuse. Cyber bullying is one of them, particularly when there are gaps in digital literacy. Older persons can not be excluded from the digital world. If our lives are going more and more online, then older persons must be able to fully participate in this realm. They must be able to exercise their rights and be protected from risks as well as enjoy the opportunities of life online. So this draft resolution isn't starting from scratch. In 2024, the Council called for the drafting of a report on this subject. but it was not compiled because of the serious liquidity crisis facing the United Nations. We believe that it is time to complete that work, but we have to do so by recognising that times have changed. The council adopted resolution 58/13, which established the intergovernmental open-ended working group tasked with drafting an internationally legally binding instrument on the rights of older persons. The first session of the group was held in July of this year. The text incorporates this change, but it doesn't obviously predict the outcome of future negotiations because it's member states that will determine the contents of that instrument through their sovereign rights. But at the same time, the issues linked to older persons' digital lives will be part of the process. We have to look at how they use digital tools and face new challenges in the digital world. That's part of today's life. In times of short resources, we need tangible mandates and this draft tries to fulfill a request made to the Council already and provide States with the appropriate basis for continuing our discussions. We don't want the report to decide for ourselves, we're hoping that the report will provide us with better information when the time comes for us to decide. That's why we call upon Member States to support this draft and consider adopting it by consensus. Thank you very much, President.

Mr. President. It's my honor to present draft resolution L21, promoting accessibility for the full enjoyment of all human rights by all, on behalf of a cross-regional core group consisting of Burundi, Cameroon, Pakistan, Turkey, and China. The draft resolution currently has 44 countries as co-sponsors. Accessibility is a symbol of progress of human civilization and provides important safeguards for all groups to participate in social life equally and conveniently. and to fully realize their human rights. Building an accessible environment originated from the care for persons with disabilities. However, as demand for accessibility grows among groups such as older persons, expectant and new mothers, children, and people who are injured or ill, the importance of accessibility for all is increasingly worthy of our attention. Accessibility for all means leaving no one behind. not only further strengthen the protection of the rights of persons with disabilities, but also ensures that the fruits of accessibility development benefit all people, achieving inclusive development that serves everyone. This is precisely the intention of this draft resolution and should also be the future direction of accessibility efforts. The draft resolution recognizes the growing need to develop accessible and age-friendly environments in the context of population aging. It notes with concern that artificial intelligence and other digital divide between and within countries continue to widen, as well as the challenges that these divide pose for many countries, in particular developing countries. It emphasizes the importance of prioritizing innovation, inclusiveness, openness, sustainability, fairness, and non-discrimin- discrimination, safety, and security in the development, deployment, and use of digital technologies. With a view to enhancing the accessibility of information and communication for all, it invites the HRC Advisory Committee to prepare a study on promoting accessibility, thereby offering a platform for relevant stakeholders to step up exchanges and international cooperation. It also provides policy guidance for countries in terms of promoting universal design, ensuring access to justice and effective legal remedies and social protection in the development of accessible environment. In the spirit of transparency, openness, and constructiveness, the core group incorporated reasonable inputs through multiple rounds of consultations and bilateral engagements and formed the current text, which is concise, balanced, and impartial. We'd like to thank the valuable contribution from all parties. It is our hope that this draft resolution could be adopted by consensus in order to move forward the cause of accessibility worldwide. I thank you, Mr. President.

Thank you. I have been informed by the Secretariat that there are 28 additional co-sponsors. I now give the floor to members of the Council who may wish to make general comments. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Pakistan, followed by Japan.

Thank you, Mr. President. Pakistan is pleased to deliver these general comments. as a member of the core group for draft resolution L.21. And we thank the delegation of China for introducing the text. The draft resolution before us is grounded in existing international human rights instruments and offers a comprehensive perspective on the positive significance of accessibility and ensuring the full enjoyment of all human rights by all. Accessibility benefits persons with disabilities, older persons and others with accessibility needs. The concept of accessibility for all reflects both current needs and the future direction of our efforts. The text recognizes the role of assistive technology and enabling participation across health, education, employment, and social protection. This connects directly to the work this council's membership has undertaken elsewhere in the UN system. Pakistan was privileged to lead the General Assembly's recent resolution on access to assistive technology. And we see the present text as complimentary. One establishing the framework, the other ensuring that accessible environments and services are available for those who rely on these devices. The draft also recognizes the potential of new and emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence to improve accessibility, while noting with concern that AI and other digital divides between and within countries continue to widen. It emphasizes innovation, inclusiveness, openness, sustainability, fairness, non-discrimination, safety and security in the development, deployment and use of these technologies. The resolution provides practical policy guidance to states, promoting universal design, ensuring access to justice and effective remedies, strengthening social protection and poverty reduction programs, and integrating accessibility into humanitarian preparedness and response. It provides for technical assistance and capacity building support to developing countries and requests the Advisory Committee to prepare a thematic report. We welcome the constructive engagement of States and stakeholders across multiple rounds of consultation on the draft text. The core group has worked transparently to arrive at a balance. The draft establishes no new mechanisms and entails no additional program budget implications, and we look forward to the Council adopting it by consensus. I thank you, Mr. President.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Japan, followed by Burundi and Gambia.

Thank you, Mr. President. Japan welcomes the constructive engagement of the core group during the informal consultation, and we join the consensus on this resolution. Third, remaining implementation gaps referred to in OP5 concern gaps in the implementation of existing international human rights treaties. Fourth, the resolution does not call for measures that go beyond the scope of the rights and obligations set forth in the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, in particular Article 9. Thank you, President. I wish to thank China for presenting L21. In addition to producing food, they preserve and hand down culture, language, customs, traditions, and collective forms of organizations, as well as the specific practices of their communities. The Declaration on the Rights of Peasants and Other Persons Working in Rural Areas was a landmark for driving forward the progressive realization of international law. The next step was the decision to establish the working group, thereby strengthening the institutional architecture of special procedures in order to ensure that there was consistent and multidimensional promotion of human rights. The experts who currently serve on the working group have taken up active roles in international fora. President.

Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, Brazil strongly supports the renewal of the mandate of the Working Group on the Rights of Peasants and Other People Working in Rural Areas. Their dedicated work is essential to translating the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Peasants and Other People Working in Rural Areas, UNDROP, from normative commitments into tangible impact on the ground. UNDROP provides an indispensable human rights framework to tackle structural inequalities in rural areas. Recognizing the central role of peasant communities, rural workers, and traditional peoples is an essential condition for eradicating hunger, preserving and sustainably using agro-biodiversity, and achieving a just ecological transition. while protecting the rights, livelihoods, and dignity of rural populations. Brazil reaffirms firmly committed to advancing public policies that address a right to food and food sovereignty, as stated by UNDROP, including the right to land and territory and the effective and meaningful participation of these groups in policy design and decision making. Thank you, President. We wish to thank the delegation of Bolivia and the core group for presenting this resolution. as a traditional co-sponsor, reasserts the need to renew the mandate of the Working Group on the Rights of Peasants and other people working in rural areas. Indeed, those who cultivate the land, who contribute to feeding the planet, must be able to benefit from development processes to preserve their dignity and to have their means of subsistence guaranteed. They help us to combat famine, to ensure food security and to preserve biodiversity. This is why we should improve their living conditions and to maintain their rights. We welcome the fact that the draft resolution pays attention to rural development, the importance of family smallholdings and the role of female farmers. That is why I wish to commend the fact that emphasis has been placed on the future of young people in farming. Thank you, Mr. President. We welcome the resolution's recognition of the indispensable contribution of peasants to food security, nutrition, biodiversity, and sustainable development. From the perspective of developing countries, it is important that the text recognizes the disproportionate impact on rural communities of poverty, climate change, drought, desertification, and economic shocks. We also value its emphasis on international cooperation, capacity building, and technology transfer in support of national efforts and rural development. We further welcome the attention accorded to smallholders, family farmers and women farmers whose contribution remains central to resilient food systems and rural livelihoods. We also note their centrality to the realization of the right to food, not only in their localities, but across the globe. Importantly, the resolution recognizes the adverse impact on rural livelihoods of inadequate access to water for peasants and rural communities, Predictable and uninterrupted access to water is essential for livelihoods, agricultural production and food security. Protecting such access, Mr. President, including where water resources are shared across borders and governed by applicable international legal obligations, is therefore paramount. Pakistan supports the adoption of L22 by consensus, and if it were to put to a vote, we will be voting in favor. I thank you, Mr. President.

Thank you, Mr. President. The Gambia is pleased to have worked together with Bolivia, Cuba, Luxembourg, and South Africa as members of the core group presenting this draft resolution. With a large agricultural population dominated by smallholder peasants, The Gambia attaches great importance to the continuation of this mandate. Peasants and other people working in rural areas continue to make vital contributions to food security, sustainable development and the preservation of biodiversity. in the face of disproportionate environmental pressures and limited access to economic and social opportunities. We welcome the improvements made to the draft resolution, including stronger recognition of the meaningful participation of peasants and rural workers in decision-making processes, policies and programmes affecting their rights. We further welcome the express recognition of women farmers and their contribution to food security and the preservation of biodiversity and traditional knowledge. Thank you, Mr. President. The United Kingdom remains firmly committed to the promotion and protection of the human rights of all individuals, including peasants and other people working in rural areas. We recognise the important contribution that rural communities make to food security, sustainable development and poverty reduction, and we support efforts to address the particular challenges they may face. The United Kingdom recognises in particular the vital role of smallholder, family and subsistence farmers. Through the UK's international development partnerships, the UK has supported agricultural productivity, climate resilience and sustainable livelihoods for rural communities across the world, helping farmers, particularly women and small-scale producers, to improve incomes and adapt to changing environmental and economic conditions. The UK has engaged constructively in discussions on this draft resolution and we would like to express our sincere appreciation to the delegation of Bolivia for the open and collaborative way in which they led the negotiation process. However, We have long-standing concerns regarding the framework underpinning this resolution, the UN Declaration on the Rights of Peasants and other people working in rural areas. Provisions of the Declaration of the Rights of Peasants seek to create new categories of rights for one specific group. This runs counter to one of the key principles enshrined in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the principle of universality. Article 1 of the UDHR, which underpins all international human rights law, states that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. We all have the same rights because we are all human. We break from that foundational principle to the detriment of us all. We therefore continue to be unable to support the mandate of a mechanism focused on the implementation of an instrument that we cannot support. The UK therefore requests a vote on this resolution and will abstain. The UK nevertheless values continued dialogue on the human rights challenges faced by rural populations, and we remain ready to work with all partners in support of efforts to promote equal access to rights, opportunities and services for all. without discrimination. Thank you, Mr. President.
